title: Eugenio Torre: Asia's first grandmaster turns 75
summary:
In 1974, Eugenio Torre became the first Asian chess player to earn the grandmaster title. At his peak, the Filipino was among the world's elite and capable of beating any of the leading players. Torre also holds the record for the most appearances at Chess Olympiads, having competed in 23 editions. He was also one of the few people to maintain a close friendship with Bobby Fischer over many years. Today, Eugenio Torre celebrates his 75th birthday. | Photo: Reykjavik Open

Eugenio Torre was born on 4 November 1951 in Iloilo City on the Philippine island of Panay. He was the seventh of his parents' ten children. His grandfather and his father were both keen chess players. His father, a lawyer by profession, taught all his children to play chess, including his son Eugenio when he was five or six years old. The children often played chess and even made their own chess pieces from scraps of leather obtained from a shoemaker. His older brothers also became strong players, but Eugenio surpassed them all with his talent.

A chess family spanning several generations

In 1958, the family moved to Quezon City in the Greater Manila area. By the age of nine, Eugenio Torre was already playing in junior tournaments, where the other youngsters were generally much older than he was. At sixteen, Torre became Philippine junior champion.

Torre made his progress entirely as a self-taught player, without any chess coach, using a few instructional books. Chess books were difficult to obtain, however. Torre learned mainly by playing through games from Chess Informant.

A chess player with a pop-star look

In 1968, Eugenio Torre played his first major international tournament in Manila. The following year, he took part in the 1969 World Junior Championship in Stockholm. Finishing fourth in his preliminary group (won by Anatoly Karpov), he missed the A final but won the B final. In 1970, Torre also won the Philippine national championship for the first time. At the 1971 World Junior Championship, he finished fourth, ahead of several strong players including Rafael Vaganian.

After finishing school, Torre began studying economics with a focus on banking and finance, but gave up his studies after two years because they could not be combined with his chess activities.

Record Olympiad participant

In 1970, Torre was selected for the Philippine team at the Chess Olympiad in Siegen. In the years that followed, Torre remained part of the Philippine squad through to the 2016 Olympiad and played in every Chess Olympiad with one exception. He did not take part in Dresden in 2008. With 23 appearances at Chess Olympiads, Eugenio Torre is therefore the record holder for Olympiad participation. In 1974 (Nice), 1980 (Valletta), 1986 (Dubai) and 2016 (Baku), he achieved the third-best result on his board and won the individual bronze medal.

The Philippine team at the 1972 Chess Olympiad in Skopje, from left: Ruben Rodriguez, Edgar De Castro, Glicerio Badilles, team official Vera and Rodolfo Tan Cardoso - Julian Lobigas is missing | Photo: Eugenio Torre on Facebook

Torre also represented the Philippines nine times at the Asian Team Championships, winning team gold four times, silver once and bronze once. On four occasions, Torre won the individual gold medal on board one. He also won one individual bronze medal.

First grandmaster from Asia

In 1972, FIDE awarded Torre the title of international master. After the Chess Olympiad in Nice, he also became the first player from Asia to receive the grandmaster title.

After winning the zonal tournament in Hong Kong in 1972, Torre qualified for the Interzonal Tournament in Leningrad, but finished only in the lower half of the standings. Nor was he able to make a stronger impression at the 1976 Interzonal in Manila. In 1979, Torre again took part in a zonal tournament. In Rio de Janeiro, he finished 7 th -9 th in a field of 18 players.

Torre achieved his best Interzonal result in Toluca in 1982, when he shared first place with Lajos Portisch.

As the first chess player from Asia, he now took part in the Candidates matches, but was eliminated in the quarterfinals by Zoltan Ribli. At the next Interzonal in 1985, Eugenio Torre again performed very well, sharing 4 th -6 th place. This was followed by a playoff for a place in the Candidates matches against Nigel Short and John van der Wiel, who had finished level on points, but Torre came last.

In 1987, Torre once again qualified for an Interzonal and, finishing seventh in Zagreb, again missed out on the Candidates matches. In 1990, Manila again hosted an Interzonal, this time played as a 64-player Swiss-system tournament. Torre, however, finished only in mid-table.

When Torre first qualified for an Interzonal tournament, he found several supporters in his home country who enabled him to undertake long journeys and play tournaments in Asia, America and, above all, Europe. Among his supporters at the time was Florencio Campomanes, who later became FIDE president. In 1972-1973, Torre lived in Madrid in order to shorten his journeys to tournaments in Europe and save on travel costs. His backers provided him with a monthly allowance of US$250.

Tournaments all over the world

Eugenio Torre took part in countless tournaments over the course of his career. In Europe, he was a welcome guest as something of an "exotic" figure. In 1977 and 1983 (fourth place), he also took part in the International German Championships in Bad Lauterberg and Hanover respectively.

Among Torre's outstanding successes were tournament victories on the Costa del Sol in 1974 and in the four-player tournament in Manila in 1976, ahead of Karpov, Ljubojevic and Browne.

Torre won the Marlboro Chess Classic in Manila in 1977, the Jakarta Internationals in 1978 and 1979 (sharing victory with Averbakh and Dorfman), the Marlboro Chess Classic in Manila in 1979, San Francisco in 1991 and Kuala Lumpur in 1994.

Who is who at the 1980 tournament in Baku? | Photo: Eugenio Torre on Facebook

In 2001, 2002 and 2014, Torre once again became Philippine national champion. In 2017, he won the Asian Senior Championship with a perfect 9/9 score.

In 1984, Torre was one of the participants in the return edition of the USSR v. Rest of the World match and won his individual match against Andrey Sokolov 2-1.

Friendship with Fischer, "Sportsman of the Millennium"

In 1974 and 1982, Eugenio Torre was named Sportsman of the Year by the Philippine sports press, and in 2000 he was named the Philippine Sportsman of the Millennium. He also received a number of other awards and honours. In 2021, he was inducted into the World Chess Hall of Fame.

Eugenio Torre was also one of the few chess players Bobby Fischer trusted and with whom the American maintained a friendship. The two first met at the 1970 Chess Olympiad in Siegen. After Fischer withdrew from public life following his World Championship victory in 1972, he also hid for a time in the Philippines. It was during this period that his close friendship with Torre developed. At the 1992 "rematch" between Fischer and Spassky, Torre served as Fischer's second and played several training games against him before the match.

Bobby Fischer in discussion with Boris Spassky, with Eugenio Torre on the left | Photo: Eugenio Torre on Facebook

At the beginning of the 2000s, Fischer even lived for a time in Baguio City, in the same residential complex as Torre.

At Fischer's grave | Photo: Eugenio Torre on Facebook

Eugenio Torre's successes played a major role in the popularity of chess in the Philippines. The 1978 World Championship match between Karpov and Korchnoi was held there, and the country hosted a Chess Olympiad in 1990. Even today, Eugenio Torre remains one of the country's greatest sporting icons. In 2023, he opened a small personal chess museum near his home in Concepcion Dos, Marikina City, where he displays memorabilia, cups and trophies from his 50-year chess career.

In 2023, Torre was appointed national coach of the Philippines and also accompanied the Philippine team to the 2024 Chess Olympiad in Budapest.

title: Bavarian Championship: 15-year-old Hussain Besou joins the leaders
summary:
Six players share the lead with 4½ points after five rounds of the Bavarian Chess Championship in Gmund am Tegernsee. The leading group includes three Indian grandmasters and 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou, who defeated former world junior champion Peter Acs in round five. Top seed Frederik Svane and third seed Alexander Donchenko are among the 31 players trailing the leaders by half a point. | Photo: Finn Engesser

Six co-leaders on 4½/5

Five rounds have been completed at the 29 th Open International Bavarian Chess Championship, a nine-round Swiss tournament taking place from 31 October to 8 November at Gut Kaltenbrunn, on the northern shore of Lake Tegernsee. Six players share the lead with 4½/5 points, including three Indian grandmasters and 15-year-old German IM Hussain Besou.

The opening two rounds saw most of the favourites make a good start , although Santos and Hungarian GM Peter Acs were both held to draws by considerably lower-rated opponents in round two. Fifty players entered the third round on perfect scores, a group that was reduced to just fourteen by the end of Monday's play.

One of the notable results in round three was 62-year-old IM Dieter Morawietz's victory over Norwegian GM Elham Amar. The 21-year-old grandmaster mixed up the move order in a line he had previously played, losing material early in the game. Morawietz, who had earned a GM norm at Tegernsee back in 2005, thus joined the leaders and occupied first place on tiebreaks. Meanwhile, Svane and Donchenko both conceded their first draws of the tournament.

Dieter Morawietz, aged 62, upset fifth seed Elham Amar | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Tuesday's fourth round saw three Indian grandmasters emerge as joint leaders with perfect 4/4 scores: G.N. Gopal, Krishnan Sasikiran and Rithvik R Raja. The latter defeated German youngster Neil Albrecht, who had previously been among the fourteen co-leaders. Behind the Indian trio, twenty players stood half a point back, including Svane, Donchenko, Morawietz and Azerbaijani GM Nijat Abasov, a participant in the 2024 Candidates Tournament.

In round five, all five games on the top boards ended in draws, leaving no player on a perfect score. Gopal and Sasikiran agreed to a draw after 31 moves in their direct encounter, while Svane, playing black against Rithvik Raja, obtained a symmetrical position and split the point after 25 moves. Donchenko also drew, against Turkish IM Eray Kilic, despite having enjoyed promising chances earlier in the game.

The main result of the day came from Besou, who defeated seventh seed Peter Acs with the white pieces. The Hungarian grandmaster, now 45, won the World Junior Championship in 2001, ten years before Besou was born. The German youngster has already established an impressive record in youth chess: he won bronze at the 2022 World Under-12 Championship, became the youngest player to represent Germany at senior level in 2023, aged eleven, and won the German under-14 title in 2024.

Besou's victory took him to 4½/5, alongside Gopal, Sasikiran, Rithvik Raja, Polish GM Kacper Piorun and Turkish GM Emre Can. The teenager is the only German representative, the only junior and the only non-GM among the six co-leaders. Piorun joined the group by defeating Morawietz, while Can benefited from a decisive mistake by IM Tobias Kügel, who lost a piece.

A further 31 players are half a point behind the leaders, including top seed Svane, third seed Donchenko, Abasov and reigning German champion Leonardo Costa. With four rounds remaining, the standings are still closely packed, while second seed Santos has more ground to make up, having collected 3½ points from his first five games.

Rithvik R Raja drew with white against top seed Frederik Svane | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

The endgame in Alexander Donchenko v. Eray Kilic attracted a lot of attention - the rating underdog held the draw after resilient defence | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

German champion Leonardo Costa and American IM Evan Park signed a 57-move draw on Wednesday | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

title: Chinese Rapid Championship: Ding Liren and Wang Hao exit in quarterfinals
summary:
Ding Liren and Wang Hao were both eliminated in the quarterfinals of the Chinese Rapid Championship, as three of the four rating favourites failed to reach the last four. Ding lost to Xiao Tong in a blitz tiebreaker, while Wang Hao was defeated by Xu Xiangyu. Yu Yangyi was the only higher-rated player to advance, joining Xiao, Xu and Lu Shanglei in the semifinals. | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

Xiao Tong and Xu Xiangyu knock out two of the big favourites

The fifth edition of the Chinese Rapid Championship is taking place in Shaoxing from 2 to 6 November, with 24 players competing in a knockout format. The field includes former world champion Ding Liren, defending champion Yu Yangyi, Wang Hao and Bu Xiangzhi, alongside a number of younger Chinese grandmasters.

Eight seeded players received byes into the round-of-16, while the remaining 16 participants contested a preliminary knockout round for the remaining eight places.

Each match consists of four rapid games, with a time control of 15 minutes plus 10-second increments. Tied matches are decided by two blitz games, with 3 minutes plus 2-second increments. If the tie remains, an Armageddon decider follows: White get 5 minutes while Black gets 4 minutes and draw odds (increments of 2 seconds are used after move 60).

Lu Miaoyi, aged 16, was knocked out by Li Di in the preliminary rounds | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

Song Yuxin was the one female player to reach the main event - she was defeated by former world champion Ding Liren in the round-of-16 | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

All games - Preliminary rounds

The round-of-16, played on Tuesday, saw all eight rating favourites advance to the quarterfinals. Five matches were settled in just three games, including comfortable victories for Ding Liren, Yu Yangyi and Wang Hao. The latter defeated Dong Hongfu 3–0, while Ding and Yu both prevailed by 2½–½ margins. Fourth seed Bu Xiangzhi needed four games to secure a 3–1 victory over the untitled Huang Renjie.

The closest contest involved two players with almost identical ratings. Xiao Tong (2476) faced Zeng Chongsheng (2475) in a match that went all the way to blitz tiebreaks. Xiao eventually prevailed 3½–2½ to complete the quarterfinal lineup.

The quarterfinals on Wednesday, however, brought a rather different set of results. Three of the four rating favourites were eliminated, including Ding Liren and Wang Hao, leaving Yu Yangyi as the only higher-rated player to reach the semifinals.

Ding's elimination came at the hands of Xiao Tong, who had already survived a lengthy match the previous day. All four rapid games ended in draws, as did the first blitz tiebreaker. In the second blitz game, Ding obtained a clear advantage with the black pieces but failed to convert it. With both players running short of time, the former world champion eventually allowed his opponent to turn the tables and win the game, securing a place in the last four.

Wang Hao also exited the competition, losing 2½–1½ to Xu Xiangyu (2594). Both players committed major blunders in games one and three, which resulted in a win apiece. The difference came in game two, when Xu obtained a convincing victory with the white pieces. He then held the draw he needed in the fourth encounter to advance.

Another upset saw Lu Shanglei (2586) defeat fourth seed Bu Xiangzhi (2593) by a 2½–1½ score. The rating difference between the two players was minimal, though. Still, Bu's elimination meant that three of the four highest-rated participants had been knocked out of the competition at the same stage.

Yu Yangyi, meanwhile, was the only rating favourite to survive the quarterfinals. He defeated Bai Jinshi 2½–1½, making the most of the white pieces to score a convincing win in the opening game before drawing the remaining three encounters. Yu faced his greatest difficulties in game four, when the players reached a complicated position featuring a queen and bishop against a rook, bishop and knight. Nevertheless, he secured the draw required to complete his match victory.

The semi-finals will see Yu Yangyi face Xu Xiangyu, while Xiao Tong takes on Lu Shanglei. Yu is now the highest-rated player remaining in the competition.

title: Firouzja Wins Titled Tuesday As Speed Chess Championship Qualifiers Confirmed
summary:
GM Alireza Firouzja won Titled Tuesday on November 3 outright with an undefeated score of 10/11, moving into second place in the 2026-27 CCT Standings. Eight players officially qualified today for the just-announced Speed Chess Championship via their performance in Titled Tuesday since September 1: GMs Hikaru Nakamura—who scored 9.5/11 today to finish second outright—Firouzja, Sina Movahed, Hans Niemann, Dmitry Andreikin, Wesley So, Denis Lazavik, and Vladislav Artemiev.

Broadcast

In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess:

Recap

Three Americans and an Iranian represented the last four perfect players after six rounds: Nakamura, Niemann, GM Fabiano Caruana, and Movahed. After seven rounds, however, there was just one: Niemann and Nakamura made a draw, but Caruana defeated Movahed to reach 7/7. After 64 moves, Caruana was down an exchange... but had five, count 'em, pawns for it. He won soon after.

Caruana's lead and perfection didn't last, as he lost in the next round to Nakamura, who became sole leader after Niemann and Firouzja drew. If anyone was pressing for the win for most of the game it was Caruana, but the game suddenly turned near the end, and now the bounty for a perfect 11/11 score moves to an even $6,000 next week.

Nakamura was able to retain his lead for one more round despite struggling for much of his game against GM Arjun Erigaisi, before Arjun blundered the game back. Niemann, Caruana, and Firouzja were able to keep within a half-point of Nakamura by defeating Movahed, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda, and GM Minh Le, respectively.

In the 10th-round encounter between Nakamura and Firouzja, Firouzja gradually began to take control around move 20 after an early mutual tactical hiccup, and he never let go from there on his way to taking the lead away from Nakamura.

At the same time, Caruana benefited from a sudden endgame turnaround to beat Niemann and keep up with Firouzja, setting up a final-round clash to determine the tournament winner. The last game proved somewhat anticlimactic, with Firouzja winning easily.

Nakamura defeated GM Maxim Matlakov to take sole second, while Niemann was able to move into third place with a win over IM Aleksandr Usov, and Caruana settled for fourth.
